title: Code Assignment Principles and Compliance

sections.learningObjectives:
- Assign diagnosis and procedure codes to the highest level of specificity supported by the documentation.
- Recognize that every code must be supported by clinician documentation in the health record.
- Apply coding compliance principles, including avoiding upcoding, downcoding, and unbundling.
- Describe how annual code updates affect code selection and office workflow.
- Identify when to query the provider and follow the practice's compliance procedures.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of specificity like a mailing address. If you know the full street, city, and zip code, you write it all down instead of just writing the country. Coding works the same way: write down as much detail as the note gives you.

### Question 2

ICD-10-CM is the big book of names for illnesses and health problems, so doctors can label what is wrong with a patient the same way everywhere.

### Question 3

If ICD-10-CM is the name of the problem, CPT is the list of actions the doctor took to help. One describes the problem, the other describes the work done.

### Question 4

Imagine a store receipt. The cashier only charges you for items actually rung up, never for things you might have wanted. Coders work from the record like a receipt: only what is written down gets coded.

### Question 5

CPT is like a dictionary of medical actions, and the American Medical Association is the team that writes and updates that dictionary.

### Question 6

Every year on October 1, the code book gets a fresh update, like a new edition of a school textbook with new pages swapped in.

### Question 7

Procedure codes get their new edition on January 1, like a calendar starting fresh at the new year.

### Question 8

A code needs at least three pieces, like a phone number needs enough digits to be dialed. More digits can be added for more detail.

### Question 9

Using last year's code book is like using last year's calendar to make an appointment; the dates no longer line up, and you show up on the wrong day.

### Question 10

The diagnosis is the reason, and the procedure is the action. You need the reason before the action makes sense, like explaining why you are baking a cake and then describing the baking you did.

### Question 11

An unspecified code is the blank 'mystery flavor' label you use only when the wrapper is torn and you cannot tell the real flavor. If the label is clear, you name the exact flavor.

### Question 12

Laterality is like saying 'right shoe' instead of just 'shoe.' It tells you which side of the body is involved.

### Question 13

Compliance is like following the rules of a game so nobody cheats; everyone codes by the same rulebook, and the scores stay fair.

### Question 14

Choosing the right code is like grading an exam; the teacher (or a trained helper) does it, not just anyone who happens to be nearby.

### Question 15

The X is like a blank spacer in a fill-in-the-blank puzzle; it holds a spot open so the important letter lands in the right place.

### Question 16

The seventh character is like a chapter marker in a story, telling you whether this is the first visit, a later follow-up, or a problem left behind after the original injury healed.

### Question 17

'Code first' is like a recipe that says to list the cause before the effect, so anyone reading knows what started the problem.

### Question 18

A combination code is like a two-for-one ticket: one code already includes both the main problem and the extra problem that comes with it.

### Question 19

Upcoding is like telling the cashier you bought the large pizza when you really ordered the small one, so you pay a bigger bill than you should.

### Question 20

Unbundling is like selling a sandwich and charging separately for the bread, the cheese, and the tomato when the menu already priced it as one sandwich.

### Question 21

Medical necessity is like only filling a prescription the doctor says you actually need, instead of grabbing every bottle off the shelf just because you can.

### Question 22

Z codes are like the 'check-in' reasons at a clinic: coming for a checkup or a screening when nothing is wrong, rather than because you are sick.

### Question 23

External cause codes are the 'story' of how someone got hurt, like the details in an accident report: what happened and where.

### Question 24

You would not follow a recipe from a torn old cookbook when the current one is right on the shelf; always use the newest, official version.

### Question 25

Downcoding is like writing down a smaller number than you actually measured on your height chart, so the record says you are shorter than you really are.

### Question 26

If the note only says 'hypertension' with no extra clues, you write down exactly that and do not fill in details that are not on the page.

### Question 27

Excludes1 is like two puzzle pieces that cannot both fit in the same spot; you choose one, not both.

### Question 28

Excludes2 is like two separate items on a menu; they are listed on different lines, but you can still order both at the same meal.

### Question 29

NOS is like writing 'some kind of fruit' on a grocery list when the note does not say whether it was an apple or a banana.

### Question 30

NEC is like a 'miscellaneous' bin; it is used when the big organized system simply has no exact drawer for that item.

### Question 31

Before the teacher grades the test, you do not know your score; you can only report what you did on each question. Coders report the symptoms they can see until the diagnosis is confirmed.

### Question 32

A combination code is like a combo meal that already includes the drink and fries; you order one item instead of listing everything separately.

### Question 33

If the note says the right leg is broken, you write 'right,' not 'one of the legs,' and definitely not 'left.'

### Question 34

If someone has both a fresh sprain and an old sore knee, you list the fresh sprain first because it is the reason they came in today.

### Question 35

Sequela is the 'aftermath' chapter: the injury is over, but it left something behind, so the record points to what remains, not the long-gone accident.

### Question 36

If a homework answer is too messy to read, you ask the teacher what it says instead of making up a score. Coders ask the doctor to clarify rather than guess.

### Question 37

You should not change your answer on a test just because a different answer is worth more points; you write the answer that is actually correct.

### Question 38

If you saw someone breaking the rules in a game, you would tell the referee, not join in or ignore it. Reporting follows the same idea.

### Question 39

You use the bus schedule that was in effect on the day you actually traveled, not the new schedule that starts the next day.

### Question 40

Category II codes are like the 'checkmarks' a teacher uses to track how the class is doing, not the grade itself.

### Question 41

Category III codes are like the 'coming soon' section of a store, tracking new items that are not yet permanent parts of the main catalog.

### Question 42

If CPT is the menu of doctor actions, HCPCS Level II is the separate list of supplies and gear, like crutches or a wheelchair, that the office might provide.

### Question 43

The level of the visit is like the length of a book report; it depends on how much work is actually shown on the page, not on how much you want to be praised.

### Question 44

The first-listed diagnosis is like the headline of a news story; it names the biggest reason the patient came in that day.

### Question 45

'Use additional code' is like a sign saying 'add the sauce on the side' so the dish is complete; you pair the second code with the first.

### Question 46

The encoder is like a spell-checker; it suggests words, but you only accept a word if it is really what the note says.

### Question 47

If a detective is not sure who took the cookies, they write down the clues they have, not a guess with a name attached.

### Question 48

You cannot turn in homework you never wrote down, even if you did the work in your head; the written record must come first.

### Question 49

A compliance program is like a sports team that practices together regularly so everyone knows the rules and plays the same way.

### Question 50

An internal audit is like checking your homework before turning it in, so you can fix mistakes before the teacher sees them.

### Question 51

A confidential hotline is like a suggestion box with a lock, so people can speak up about problems without worrying about getting in trouble.

### Question 52

If both shoes have holes, you report both shoes, not just one, and you say 'both' rather than leaving it unclear.

### Question 53

Unbundling is like a restaurant charging you separately for the bun, patty, and cheese when the menu already lists them as one burger combo.

### Question 54

Using an unspecified code when you have detail is like labeling a package 'stuff' when you know exactly what is inside; you lose useful information.

### Question 55

Coding information is like a diary with a patient's private details; you keep it closed and share it only with the right people.

### Question 56

If you cannot read a messy note, you ask the person who wrote it instead of guessing what it says.

### Question 57

The diagnosis is the 'why' and the procedure is the 'what'; they must match, like a receipt showing why each purchase was needed.

### Question 58

An injury claim is like an accident report: you write what got hurt and also the story of how and where it happened.

### Question 59

Coding is writing the shorthand labels for what happened; billing is the person who mails those labels in to get paid, like translating an order and then sending the invoice.

### Question 60

The index is the map that points you to a page, and the tabular list is the actual page where you confirm the full, correct address.

### Question 61

Every code is like a data point in a giant survey; when the answers are correct, scientists and health officials can see the real picture of the nation's health.

### Question 62

Coding guidelines are like the rules of a board game; everyone follows the same instructions so the game is fair and makes sense.

### Question 63

Every diagnosis code starts with a letter, like a book title starting with a capital letter before the rest of the details follow.

### Question 64

'See also' is like a librarian saying, 'You might also check the shelf next door,' giving you another place to look without forcing you to use it.

### Question 65

'Initial' is about active treatment, not the literal first visit; as long as the doctor is still actively fixing the break, it stays in the 'initial' chapter.

### Question 66

A 'history of' code is like a note in a diary saying something happened long ago but is over now; you do not write it as if it is happening today.

### Question 67

A screening visit is like a safety inspection for a car that is running fine; you record the inspection, not an imaginary breakdown.

### Question 68

If you say you have a peanut butter and jelly sandwich, you do not separately say you have jelly; it is already included in the sandwich.

### Question 69

The X is a spacer that holds a spot open, like a placeholder chair that keeps a seat for the seventh character to sit in the right spot.

### Question 70

If the note says the water is 'warm,' you write 'warm,' not 'boiling,' even though warm water can sometimes get hotter.

### Question 71

You write the grade based on this week's test, not on last year's report card or what another student scored.

### Question 72

A code needs a signed 'receipt' from the doctor in the official record; a note that is not saved and signed does not count.

### Question 73

If two pages of a story disagree, you ask the author which version is right instead of telling both versions as if both happened.

### Question 74

When two items are tied for first place, the rulebook says either one may go first; you just follow the rule, not the prize money.

### Question 75

If the store accidentally overcharged a customer, the right move is to give the money back and fix the register, not keep quiet and repeat the mistake.

### Question 76

An error is dropping a plate by accident; fraud is throwing it on purpose. Both break the plate, but only one was done on purpose.

### Question 77

If auto-correct suggests a vague word but you know the exact one, you type the exact word; the tool does not decide for you.

### Question 78

When an old injury leaves a limp, you write the limp first (what is happening now), then a note that it came from the old injury (the cause).

### Question 79

'Subsequent' is the follow-up chapter: the first fix is done, and now the patient comes back for regular check-ins while everything heals.

### Question 80

If someone has a cold and also mentions a sore ankle, you write down both, because the sore ankle is not part of the cold.

### Question 81

If a routine safety check turns up a loose wire, you write down both the check you did and the loose wire you found.

### Question 82

You write the broken bone first, then add the 'how it happened' detail after, like listing the main event and then the backstory.

### Question 83

If a cake comes out burnt, you do not write 'normal baking' on the report; you note that something went wrong.

### Question 84

After the storm has passed, you write 'cleanup and repair' instead of still writing 'storm in progress.'

### Question 85

If you cannot buy a combo meal, you order the main dish first and the side second, in the order the menu requires.

### Question 86

Switching to new codes is like switching to a new calendar: everyone gets the updated one and starts using it together on the correct day.

### Question 87

Before mailing a package, you check that everything on the shipping list is actually in the box; if something is missing, you stop and fix it first.

### Question 88

If the same mistake keeps happening, the smart fix is to retrain the team and check the work, not to hide it or blame one person.

### Question 89

If two notes say 'right' and 'left,' you ask which one is correct rather than picking based on which came first.

### Question 90

If a note just says 'big animal,' you ask whether it was a horse or an elephant instead of guessing, so the record says the right thing.
